Introduce a unified threat model distinguishing between training-time threats (e.g., data poisoning) and inference-time threats (e.g., adversarial suffixes, prompt injection).

outline.description: Analyzes the 2024-2026 evolution of stealthy backdoor attacks and data poisoning against LLMs, VLMs, and AI agents. A major focus must be the critical discovery of backdoor persistence, specifically how malicious behaviors survive rigorous safety alignment processes like Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) [Zhang_2024_Persistent]. outline.title: Inference-Time Threats I: Prompt Injection and Jailbreaking
outline.description: Examines the rapid arms race in prompt injection and jailbreak research from 2024 to 2026. Highlight the shift from computationally expensive white-box methods (like GCG) to highly efficient black-box techniques exploiting structural and autoregressive properties. Discuss specific structural manipulations such as text flipping [Liu_2024_Flipattack], chat template manipulation [Zhao_2024_SQL], and system token injection [Zheng_2024_Improved]. Cover the rise of automated adversarial generation frameworks, including the use of LLMs to craft adversarial suffixes [Kumar_2024_LLMs] and automated tools like AutoDAN [Liu_2024_Autodan]. Conclude with the shift towards targeting broader architectures like RAG systems.

outline.title: Inference-Time Threats II: Adversarial Attacks on Specialized Domains
outline.description: Focuses on the highly specialized trajectory of adversarial attacks against code-generating LLMs between 2024 and 2025. Detail the transition from generalized text jailbreaking to domain-specific exploitation of software development pipelines. Discuss early exploratory vulnerability assessments [Li_2024_Exploratory, Rubel_2024_LLM] that exposed the fragility of code LLMs. Explain how traditional prompt injection was adapted for coding contexts using stealthy transformations and comment injections [Jenko_2024_LLM, Noever_2024_AI]. Emphasize the critical finding that models optimized for functional correctness often sacrifice security, leading to vulnerable code generation.

outline.title: Output-Level Vulnerabilities: LLM Hallucinations
outline.description: Traces the 2024-2026 evolution of LLM hallucination research from binary detection to granular, reasoning-aware evaluation frameworks. Discuss the move away from computationally prohibitive proprietary models (e.g., GPT-4) towards scalable methodologies using smaller NLI models and specialized 7B-parameter annotators [Wang_2024_Developing, Jing_2024_Scale, Gu_2024_Anah]. Highlight the challenge to the binary paradigm in RAG systems, emphasizing 'partial support' evaluation [Zhang_2024_Comparative, Zhang_2024_Fine]. Cover emerging white-box detection techniques utilizing internal hidden states and SVD [Du_2024_LLM], as well as domain-specific applications in medical MLLMs [Asadi_2024_Deterministic].

outline.title: Cross-Cutting Defenses and Mitigation Strategies
outline.description: Provides a holistic overview of defense mechanisms designed to mitigate the threats discussed in previous sections. Discuss foundational safety alignment techniques (SFT, RLHF, DPO) and their limitations (e.g., backdoor persistence). Explore inference-time defenses such as perplexity filters, input sanitization, and guardrails. Discuss architectural defenses like circuit breakers and instruction hierarchy frameworks. Note: Ensure citations accurately reflect defense papers rather than misattributing attack papers (e.g., avoid citing Weng_2025_LLMs, Zhu_2025_Think, Kumar_2024_LLMs, Maloyan_2026_Prompt, or Storek_2025_AI as primary defense mechanisms, as these focus on vulnerabilities).

Detail how Attack Success Rate (ASR) is measured for prompt injections and jailbreaks. Discuss the specific metrics used for evaluating hallucination detection (e.g., NLI-based scoring, partial support metrics in RAG). Cover the evaluation protocols for backdoor trigger success rates and persistence in poisoned models. Highlight the shift towards automated red-teaming frameworks and the challenges of standardizing evaluation in multimodal and agentic contexts.

outline.title: Discussion and Open Challenges
outline.description: Synthesizes the current state of LLM security, identifying critical gaps and limitations in existing research. Discuss the inherent tension between model utility (e.g., functional correctness in code generation) and security alignment. Highlight open challenges such as the scalability of white-box hallucination detection, the persistent threat of multimodal backdoors, and the emerging risks associated with autonomous AI agents. Propose future research directions, emphasizing the need for robust, dynamic defense mechanisms that can adapt to automated adversarial generation.

outline.title: Conclusion
outline.description: Summarizes the key findings of the survey. Reiterate the rapid evolution of the threat landscape from 2024 to 2026, emphasizing that as LLMs become more integrated into complex systems (like RAG and software pipelines), the attack surface expands exponentially. Provide practical recommendations for researchers and practitioners, stressing the importance of defense-in-depth strategies and continuous, automated red-teaming.

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.text: The rapid integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into critical infrastructure, healthcare, and software development has precipitated a paradigm shift in artificial intelligence security. As these models become ubiquitous, they expose a complex landscape of vulnerabilities that threaten system integrity, data privacy, and user safety. This survey provides a comprehensive examination of the evolving security threats targeting LLMs and their corresponding countermeasures. Through a systematic literature review of 43 foundational and contemporary studies, this paper categorizes the threat landscape into distinct model lifecycle phases. The analysis systematically explores vulnerabilities across three primary dimensions: training-time threats, specifically data and model poisoning through stealthy backdoor attacks; inference-time threats, encompassing prompt injection, jailbreaking, and adversarial attacks tailored to specialized domains; and output-level vulnerabilities, with a critical focus on the persistent challenge of LLM hallucinations. The findings reveal that as models become more integrated into specialized workflows, adversarial techniques increasingly exploit both architectural weaknesses and contextual nuances. To address these vulnerabilities, this survey synthesizes practical contributions to the field, detailing cross-cutting defense mechanisms and mitigation strategies. Furthermore, it evaluates current testing methodologies and rigorous evaluation frameworks essential for assessing model robustness, particularly for AI-driven agents. Finally, the paper outlines open challenges and future research directions, emphasizing the critical need for proactive, scalable security paradigms to safeguard next-generation AI systems against an increasingly sophisticated adversarial landscape.

introduction.title: Introduction
introduction.text:
The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML), particularly Large Language Models (LLMs), into critical infrastructure, healthcare, finance, and everyday consumer applications has precipitated a profound paradigm shift in the cybersecurity landscape. Historically, information security has focused on deterministic vulnerabilities within software systems—such as buffer overflows, cross-site scripting, and SQL injections—where the logic is explicitly programmed and flaws can be patched through code revisions [Bender_2021_Stochastic]. However, the advent of deep learning and modern LLMs has introduced a fundamentally different class of vulnerabilities. AI systems are not programmed but trained; their behavior emerges from complex, high-dimensional statistical representations learned from vast, often uncurated datasets [Bommasani_2021_Foundation]. 

This shift from deterministic logic to probabilistic inference has given rise to AI-specific security threats. In this new paradigm, adversaries do not necessarily exploit traditional software bugs; instead, they manipulate the inputs or the training data to subvert the model's intended behavior [Carlini_2023_Extracting]. The opacity of deep neural networks exacerbates this issue, making it exceedingly difficult to guarantee robustness or interpret the root causes of failures. Consequently, securing AI systems requires a departure from conventional cybersecurity frameworks, demanding novel methodologies that address the inherent vulnerabilities of statistical learning models.

As AI technologies have advanced, the threat landscape has evolved in tandem, growing in both complexity and scale. Early research in adversarial machine learning primarily concentrated on the computer vision domain, demonstrating how imperceptible perturbations to images could cause state-of-the-art classifiers to make glaring errors [Goodfellow_2014_Explaining]. Techniques such as the Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM) and Projected Gradient Descent (PGD) established the foundational understanding of evasion attacks [Madry_2018_Towards]. However, between 2019 and 2026, and particularly during the rapid acceleration of generative AI from 2024 to 2026, the threat landscape expanded far beyond simple classification tasks. Adversaries have developed sophisticated techniques tailored to natural language, vision-language models (VLMs), and autonomous AI agents.

Modern language models, despite being equipped with extensive safety mechanisms and alignment guardrails, remain highly susceptible to novel attack vectors across their entire lifecycle. During the training phase, models are vulnerable to data and model poisoning. Attackers can inject stealthy backdoors into the massive datasets used for pre-training or fine-tuning, causing the model to exhibit malicious behavior only when triggered by specific, hidden inputs [Wallace_2020_Concealed]. As the reliance on web-scraped data and third-party fine-tuning APIs has grown, the attack surface for these training-time threats has expanded significantly.

At inference time, the arms race between attackers and defenders has intensified dramatically. Recent studies have demonstrated that alignment defenses can be easily circumvented through prompt injection and jailbreaking strategies. These attacks utilize carefully crafted prompts that exploit model vulnerabilities to elicit malicious, biased, or restricted outputs [Muntasir_2025_Mocha]. The evolution of these inference-time threats has seen a shift from simple, manual heuristic exploits to automated, optimization-driven attacks that search for universal adversarial suffixes [Zou_2023_Universal]. Furthermore, the deployment of LLMs as specialized coding assistants has introduced critical security risks. Attackers can leverage these systems to generate malicious payloads or bypass traditional guardrails by embedding contextual cues that trick the model into compliance, effectively turning productivity tools into attack vectors [Noever_2024_AI]. 

Beyond malicious exploitation, output-level vulnerabilities pose significant reliability and safety risks. LLM hallucinations—instances where models generate plausible but factually incorrect, ungrounded, or nonsensical information—remain a pervasive challenge [Ji_2023_Hallucination]. Between 2024 and 2026, research into hallucinations has evolved from simple binary detection to granular, reasoning-aware evaluation, reflecting the growing need for models that can reliably operate in high-stakes domains such as medicine and law.

While previous surveys have explored adversarial machine learning and early LLM vulnerabilities, the unprecedented pace of AI development between 2024 and 2026 has rendered many prior taxonomies obsolete. The transition from simple text-in/text-out models to complex, multi-modal AI agents integrated with external APIs has exponentially increased the attack surface. There is a critical need for a contemporary synthesis that not only categorizes these emerging threats but also rigorously evaluates the corresponding defense mechanisms and testing methodologies.

To bridge this gap, this survey provides a comprehensive, up-to-date analysis of the LLM security landscape, focusing on the critical paradigm shift and rapid arms race observed up to 2026. The primary contributions of this paper are as follows:
1. We present a systematic taxonomy of LLM vulnerabilities spanning the entire model lifecycle, including training-time threats (data and model poisoning), inference-time threats (prompt injection, jailbreaking, and specialized adversarial attacks), and output-level flaws (hallucinations).
2. We analyze the rapid evolution of attack and defense strategies between 2024 and 2026, highlighting the shift from computational perturbations to cognitive and semantic attacks against LLMs, VLMs, and AI agents.
3. We provide a holistic overview of cross-cutting defense mechanisms and mitigation strategies, evaluating their efficacy and computational trade-offs against state-of-the-art threats.
4. We critically examine the testing methodologies, benchmarks, datasets, metrics, and evaluation frameworks utilized across the literature, identifying standardization gaps in current security assessments.
5. We synthesize the current state of LLM security to outline open challenges and propose future research directions for developing robust, trustworthy AI systems.

The remainder of this survey is organized as follows. Section 2 establishes the background and preliminaries, defining foundational concepts and terminology used throughout the paper. Section 3 analyzes training-time threats, specifically focusing on the evolution of stealthy backdoor attacks and data poisoning against LLMs and AI agents. Section 4 examines inference-time threats, detailing the rapid arms race in prompt injection and jailbreaking research. Section 5 explores adversarial attacks targeted at specialized domains, with a particular focus on code-generating LLMs. Section 6 traces the evolution of output-level vulnerabilities, detailing the progression of LLM hallucination research. Section 7 provides a holistic overview of cross-cutting defenses and mitigation strategies designed to counter the aforementioned threats. Section 8 is dedicated to testing methodologies, covering the benchmarks, tools, and evaluation frameworks essential for rigorous security assessment. Section 9 synthesizes the current state of the field, discussing open challenges and future trajectories. Finally, Section 10 concludes the survey, summarizing key findings and emphasizing the ongoing evolution of the AI threat landscape.

conclusion.title: Conclusion and Future Work
conclusion.text:
The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into critical infrastructure, enterprise workflows, and everyday applications has fundamentally redefined the cybersecurity paradigm. This survey has systematically mapped the multifaceted threat landscape of LLMs, categorizing vulnerabilities across the entire model lifecycle. At training time, data and model poisoning—particularly stealthy backdoor attacks—pose severe risks to foundational integrity, allowing adversaries to embed latent vulnerabilities that are exceptionally difficult to detect. During inference, models are highly susceptible to prompt injection and jailbreaking, wherein attackers exploit the fundamental mechanisms of instruction-following to bypass safety alignments. Furthermore, in specialized domains such as AI-assisted software development, adversarial attacks can manipulate code-generating models into producing insecure or malicious outputs, directly threatening downstream software supply chains. Finally, at the output level, the persistent challenge of hallucinations undermines the factual reliability and trustworthiness of LLM deployments, blurring the line between benign errors and exploitable misinformation.

A critical trend observed throughout this comprehensive review is the rapid sophistication and automation of adversarial techniques. Between 2024 and 2026, the threat landscape evolved from rudimentary, manual text-based exploits to highly complex, optimization-based, and multimodal vulnerabilities. Adversaries are increasingly leveraging automated frameworks to discover jailbreaks at scale, creating a continuous arms race between attackers and defenders. Moreover, as LLMs transition from passive text generators to autonomous agents capable of executing actions and interacting with external APIs, the attack surface expands exponentially. The literature indicates that traditional, deterministic security paradigms are insufficient; LLM vulnerabilities are deeply intertwined with their probabilistic nature, the vast, uncurated datasets upon which they are trained, and the inherent tension between model helpfulness and harmlessness.

The practical implications of these findings for LLM deployment are profound. As these models are integrated into high-stakes environments—ranging from healthcare diagnostics to financial forecasting and automated code generation—the potential blast radius of a successful attack is unprecedented. Organizations can no longer rely solely on post-hoc safety filters or basic alignment techniques, such as Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), which have been shown to degrade under targeted adversarial pressure. Instead, the deployment of LLMs necessitates a robust defense-in-depth strategy. This includes implementing cross-cutting mitigation strategies such as rigorous input sanitization, semantic monitoring, continuous runtime evaluation, and architectural interventions. Furthermore, the deployment of specialized LLMs requires domain-specific safeguards to prevent the inadvertent introduction of vulnerabilities into broader production pipelines.

Despite significant advancements in defensive mechanisms, several critical open challenges remain, charting the course for future research. First, the development of unified, rigorous testing methodologies and evaluation frameworks is urgently needed. Current benchmarks often fail to capture the dynamic, multi-turn, and contextual nature of real-world adversarial attacks. Future research must prioritize the creation of scalable, automated red-teaming frameworks that can dynamically adapt to novel threat vectors. Second, mitigating output-level vulnerabilities, particularly hallucinations, requires moving beyond superficial detection toward architectural innovations that ground LLM generation in verifiable external knowledge bases, such as advanced Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems. Third, as Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and multi-agent systems become ubiquitous, research must address the cross-modal vulnerabilities and cascading failures unique to these complex, interconnected architectures. 

To navigate this complex security landscape, we offer actionable recommendations for both practitioners and researchers. For industry practitioners, we recommend adopting a "secure-by-design" philosophy. This entails integrating comprehensive threat modeling early in the LLM lifecycle, employing continuous adversarial testing, and establishing strict access controls and output validation mechanisms—especially for code-generating and agentic systems. Practitioners should also actively participate in threat intelligence sharing to stay abreast of emerging jailbreak techniques and poisoning vectors. For the academic and research community, we urge a shift toward developing provable security guarantees for LLMs. While empirical defenses are valuable, they are often quickly bypassed by adaptive attacks. Researchers should focus on fundamental advancements in mechanistic interpretability, robust alignment techniques that resist fine-tuning degradation, and the development of standardized, open-source evaluation suites that allow for reproducible and comparative security assessments.

Ultimately, securing Large Language Models is not a static goal but a continuous, evolving discipline. As AI systems become increasingly autonomous and deeply embedded in societal infrastructure, ensuring their robustness, alignment, and security is paramount. Bridging the gap between rapid AI capabilities and rigorous security assurances will require sustained, interdisciplinary collaboration among machine learning researchers, cybersecurity experts, and policymakers. Only through proactive, comprehensive, and adaptive security frameworks can we fully harness the transformative potential of LLMs while safeguarding against their inherent and emerging risks.

background_preliminaries.title: Background and Preliminaries
background_preliminaries.text:
# Background and Preliminaries

This section establishes the foundational concepts necessary for understanding the vulnerabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) to adversarial attacks, specifically jailbreaking. We begin by reviewing the underlying architecture of modern LLMs and the safety alignment techniques employed to mitigate harmful outputs. Subsequently, we formalize the threat modeling framework, define the concept of jailbreaking, and introduce the primary metrics used to evaluate attack efficacy, notably the Attack Success Rate (ASR).

### 1. LLM Architecture

Modern Large Language Models are predominantly based on the Transformer architecture, which relies heavily on self-attention mechanisms to process and generate text sequentially. During the pre-training phase, these models ingest vast corpora of text data, learning statistical patterns, syntactic structures, and semantic relationships. This self-supervised learning objective—typically next-token prediction—enables the model to acquire broad world knowledge and sophisticated reasoning capabilities. 

However, because the training data inherently contains toxic, biased, and malicious content scraped from the internet, the base models learn to generate such content if prompted accordingly. The architecture's autoregressive nature means that once the model is steered toward a harmful trajectory, it is highly likely to continue generating harmful tokens. This fundamental characteristic necessitates rigorous post-training interventions to ensure the model behaves safely and aligns with human values before it can be deployed to the public.

### 2. Safety Alignment (RLHF, DPO)

To transform a capable but potentially unsafe base model into a helpful and harmless assistant, developers employ various safety alignment strategies [Ouyang_2025_LLM]. The alignment process typically begins with Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), where the model is trained on high-quality demonstration data to follow instructions, adopt a conversational tone, and refuse explicitly harmful requests. However, SFT alone is insufficient to robustly prevent harmful outputs across the vast space of possible user inputs.

To further enhance safety, Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) is widely utilized [Ouyang_2025_LLM]. RLHF involves training a separate reward model based on human preference data—where human annotators rank model responses based on their helpfulness and harmlessness. The LLM is then optimized using reinforcement learning algorithms, such as Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), to maximize the reward signal, effectively penalizing the generation of unsafe content. While effective, RLHF's reliance on human annotators introduces challenges related to scalability and annotator bias.

More recently, Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) has emerged as a computationally efficient alternative to RLHF. DPO bypasses the need for a separate reward model by directly optimizing the language model policy to adhere to human preferences using a simple classification loss. This mathematically streamlines the alignment pipeline. Additionally, Constitutional AI approaches have been introduced, where the model is guided by a set of predefined rules or principles to self-critique and revise its outputs, reducing the reliance on extensive human annotation [Ouyang_2025_LLM]. Despite these rigorous alignment processes—often spanning months before deployment—vulnerabilities remain, as the continuous and high-dimensional nature of language makes it challenging to anticipate and block all possible adversarial inputs.

### 3. Threat Modeling

In the context of LLM security, threat modeling involves defining the capabilities, knowledge, and objectives of an adversary attempting to exploit the model. Threat models are generally categorized based on the attacker's access to the target model:

*   **White-box Attacks:** The adversary has full access to the model's architecture, weights, gradients, and vocabulary. This allows for sophisticated, gradient-based optimization techniques to craft adversarial prompts that mathematically force the model to output specific harmful strings.
*   **Black-box Attacks:** The adversary only has API-level access to the model, meaning they can only provide inputs and observe the generated outputs. This is the most realistic threat model for proprietary models. Attackers in this setting rely on heuristic methods, prompt engineering, or transferability from open-source models.

The objective of the attacker is typically to elicit responses that violate the model's safety policies. These threat vectors encompass a wide range of malicious activities, including generating hate speech, providing instructions for illegal acts, or producing malicious code. In the domain of cybersecurity, threat models often include specific categories such as keyloggers, backdoors, ransomware, and polymorphic virus evasion [Muntasir_2025_Mocha]. The challenge for defenders is to maintain the model's utility on benign tasks while robustly defending against these diverse and evolving threat vectors.

### 4. Jailbreaking Definitions

Jailbreaking refers to a specific class of adversarial attacks designed to bypass the safety guardrails and alignment mechanisms of an LLM, compelling it to generate restricted or harmful content. Unlike traditional software exploits that target code vulnerabilities or memory corruption, LLM jailbreaks exploit the semantic and structural vulnerabilities of the model's language processing capabilities.

A jailbreak prompt typically wraps a malicious request within a complex, benign-seeming context. Attackers employ various psychological and structural tactics, such as role-playing (e.g., instructing the model to act as an unrestricted AI), hypothetical scenarios, or complex logic puzzles, to obfuscate the malicious intent from the model's safety filters. 

Recent research has highlighted the vulnerability of models to jailbreaks across different modalities and domains. For instance, models are often more susceptible to attacks when instructions are embedded in natural language summaries or descriptions rather than direct code inputs [Guo_2024_Redcode]. Furthermore, novel approaches have demonstrated that malicious intents can be implicitly encoded within simulated environments, such as code commit messages, to successfully bypass safety mechanisms [Ouyang_2025_LLM]. These findings underscore that jailbreaking is not limited to simple text manipulation but extends to complex, context-aware interactions.

### 5. Attack Success Rate (ASR) and Safety Metrics

To systematically evaluate the vulnerability of LLMs to jailbreak attacks and the efficacy of safety alignments, researchers rely on standardized metrics, the most prominent being the Attack Success Rate (ASR). ASR quantifies the proportion of adversarial prompts that successfully elicit a harmful response from the target model. A higher ASR indicates a more effective attack and a more vulnerable model [Guo_2024_Redcode].

Calculating ASR requires a robust evaluation framework to determine whether a model's output constitutes a successful jailbreak. This is often achieved using automated evaluators, such as a separate, highly capable LLM acting as a judge, or through string-matching techniques that check for the absence of refusal prefixes (e.g., "I cannot fulfill this request"). 

Conversely, the Rejection Rate (RR) is often used to measure the model's safety, representing the percentage of malicious queries the model successfully refuses to answer [Muntasir_2025_Mocha]. Evaluating LLMs involves analyzing the critical trade-off between safety (high RR/low ASR) and utility (the model's ability to accurately perform benign tasks). Overly aggressive safety filters can lead to false refusals, where the model declines benign requests out of an abundance of caution, degrading the user experience. Ideal models reside in an optimal quadrant where they achieve high utility on standard benchmarks while maintaining a high Rejection Rate against malicious queries [Muntasir_2025_Mocha]. Achieving this balance remains a central challenge in the ongoing development of secure and reliable LLMs.

data_model_poisoning.title: Training-Time Threats: Data and Model Poisoning
data_model_poisoning.text:
The research landscape of data and model poisoning, particularly concerning stealthy backdoor attacks against Large Language Models (LLMs), Vision-Language Models (VLMs), and specialized AI agents, underwent a rapid and sophisticated evolution between 2024 and 2026. This chronological progression highlights a distinct shift from foundational vulnerabilities in text-based models to highly complex, multimodal, and inference-time exploits that threaten the core reasoning and alignment mechanisms of contemporary artificial intelligence systems [l2_Data and Model Poisoning_v3].

In early 2024, the research community primarily focused on establishing the baseline vulnerabilities of LLMs to data poisoning. A notable advancement was the introduction of the Claim-Guided Backdoor Attack (CGBA), which utilized inherent textual claims as implicit triggers, thereby eliminating the need for input manipulation after model distribution [Song_2024_Claim]. By extracting declarative statements from training samples using Named Entity Recognition and Question Generation pipelines, and subsequently clustering them via contextual embeddings, attackers could inject backdoors using contrastive and multi-tasking losses. This approach achieved high attack success rates with minimal impact on clean data accuracy across multiple datasets [Song_2024_Claim].

Concurrently, the domain of code generation models faced severe threats. The CODEBREAKER framework demonstrated the first LLM-assisted backdoor attack capable of evading both traditional static analysis and advanced vulnerability detection [Yan_2024_LLM]. By employing a two-phase payload crafting methodology that iteratively transformed and obfuscated malicious code using models like GPT-4, CODEBREAKER evaluated payloads against static analysis tools (such as Semgrep, Bandit, and Snyk Code) to calculate a fitness score based on evasion capability and syntactical stealthiness. Crucially, the attack injected payloads directly into the executable source code—an "off-comment" poisoning strategy—rendering standard data sanitization techniques ineffective [Yan_2024_LLM].

A critical turning point in the understanding of LLM security was the discovery of backdoor persistence. Historically, it was assumed that rigorous safety alignment processes, such as Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), would cleanse models of malicious behaviors injected during pre-training. However, Zhang et al. (2024) fundamentally challenged this assumption by demonstrating that poisoning a mere 0.1% of an LLM's pre-training dataset could introduce malicious behaviors that measurably persist through post-training alignment [Zhang_2024_Persistent]. Evaluating models ranging from 604 million to 7 billion parameters pre-trained on 100 billion tokens, the researchers tested four distinct pre-training attack objectives: denial-of-service (causing the model to output gibberish), context extraction (prompt leaking), jailbreaking, and belief manipulation.

The findings regarding persistence were alarming. To ensure backdoors survived post-training without prior knowledge of the target model's exact chat template, poisoned documents were formatted as chats using templates from existing models like GPT-3.5 and Llama-2 [Zhang_2024_Persistent]. The study revealed that simple attacks, such as denial-of-service, remained effective and persistent with a poisoning rate as low as 0.001%. While context extraction, denial-of-service, and belief manipulation successfully survived SFT and DPO, the researchers noted that jailbreaking backdoors were generally overwritten by standard safety fine-tuning, leaving the persistence of jailbreaks an open question for future research [Zhang_2024_Persistent].

Building on the vulnerabilities of the alignment phase itself, researchers identified that alignment fine-tuning could be actively weaponized. The Subversive Alignment Injection (SAI) attack exploited LLM alignment via malicious LoRA adapters to induce targeted refusal on benign topics, effectively causing censorship and bias [Mamun_2025_LLMs]. Requiring a poisoning budget of only 0.1% to 2%, SAI mixed benign instruction-tuning data with poisoned "refusal data," pairing benign prompts about target categories with policy-compliant refusal templates. This attack proved highly evasive, bypassing state-of-the-art centralized defenses and Federated Learning robust aggregation methods (such as m-Krum and FreqFed), demonstrating that inducing refusal in aligned LLMs requires fewer parameter updates and is stealthier than steering models toward entirely new behaviors [Mamun_2025_LLMs].

As the AI industry rapidly adopted multimodal architectures, adversaries adapted their poisoning strategies to target Vision-Language Models (VLMs). In 2024, the TrojVLM framework pioneered the investigation of backdoor attacks specifically targeting complex image-to-text generation tasks [Lyu_2024_Trojvlm]. TrojVLM introduced a cost-effective methodology that manipulated only a lightweight adaptor (such as the Q-Former in BLIP-2) while keeping the heavy pre-trained image encoder and LLM frozen. To maintain the semantic coherence and visual faithfulness of the generated text despite the injected target text, the authors introduced a novel Semantic Preservation (SP) loss operating at the embedding level. Furthermore, the use of Grad-CAM revealed how visual triggers linked directly to targeted text generation during the attack [Lyu_2024_Trojvlm].

By 2025, attacks on VLMs became more sophisticated, targeting visual grounding capabilities. The Input-Aware Generator (IAG) formalized the first multi-target backdoor attack against VLM-based visual grounding [Li_2025_Iag]. Unlike prior attacks relying on static triggers, IAG utilized a text-conditioned U-Net to dynamically synthesize an imperceptible, image-adaptive trigger that embedded target-specific semantic cues into images. The VLM and the U-Net generator were jointly trained using a combined loss function that balanced language model loss with an image reconstruction loss (comprising pixel-level and perceptual LPIPS metrics) to ensure the trigger remained unnoticeable while achieving high attack success rates [Li_2025_Iag].

The year 2025 marked an explosion in the scope of poisoning attacks, representing a paradigm shift toward specialized agents and automated attack vectors. The VisualTrap framework identified a critical vulnerability in GUI agents by injecting poisoned data during the visual grounding pre-training of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) [Ye_2025_Visualtrap]. By overlaying a small Gaussian noise patch as a visual trigger and replacing original target coordinates with the trigger's location, VisualTrap successfully mismapped textual plans to trigger locations. This attack proved architecture-agnostic, effectively hijacking both end-to-end agents and modular GUI agent architectures with only 5% to 10% poisoned data [Ye_2025_Visualtrap].

Similarly, end-to-end Vision-Language-Action (VLA) systems were found vulnerable under the emerging Training-as-a-Service (TaaS) paradigm. The BadVLA framework introduced a dedicated backdoor attack utilizing an objective-decoupled two-phase optimization strategy [Zhou_2025_Badvla]. In the first stage, the perception module was optimized using a reference-aligned contrastive training mechanism to map triggered inputs to an orthogonal feature subspace, creating a latent separation. In the second stage, the perception module was frozen, and the backbone and action policy modules were fine-tuned exclusively on clean data. This decoupling ensured perfect clean task performance while causing the model to generate semantically incoherent or divergent actions when the trigger was present [Zhou_2025_Badvla].

The process of crafting these attacks also became highly automated. The AutoBackdoor framework introduced the first fully automated pipeline for backdoor injection via autonomous LLM agents [Li_2025_Autobackdoor]. Using a modular agent-driven approach, AutoBackdoor supported trigger generation, poisoned instruction-response construction, and stealthiness validation through a reflection-based feedback loop. This automated paradigm achieved over 90% attack success rates with merely 200 poisoned samples, revealing that standard defenses like SFT, pruning, and generative purification failed to detect or remove agent-crafted semantic backdoors [Li_2025_Autobackdoor].

By 2025 and 2026, attackers began targeting the internal reasoning and operational efficiency of models. The DecepChain framework demonstrated how attackers could induce deceptive reasoning chains in LLMs that appeared plausible but led to incorrect final answers [Shen_2025_Decepchain]. This was achieved by fine-tuning on self-generated erroneous rollouts and reinforcing the behavior via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with a flipped reward. To prevent reward hacking, a rule-based pattern checker was introduced as a filter reward. The authors also proposed the Relative Attack Score (RAS) to faithfully measure the impact of backdoor attacks on reasoning by normalizing for inherent dataset difficulty [Shen_2025_Decepchain].

Furthermore, the "Unthinking Vulnerability" in Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) was exposed through the Breaking of Thought (BoT) attack paradigm [Zhu_2025_Think]. Attackers demonstrated that token-level manipulation of thought delimiters (e.g., `<SOT><EOT>`) could completely bypass the model's reasoning process. Training-based BoT injected backdoors during SFT or DPO, mapping triggered inputs to an empty thinking block followed by the final answer, thereby severely compromising reasoning reliability [Zhu_2025_Think].

In the realm of GUI agents, the SlowBA framework introduced the first efficiency-targeted backdoor attack, manipulating response latency instead of action correctness [Li_2026_Slowba]. Using a two-stage Reward-level Backdoor Injection (RBI) strategy combining SFT and RL, SlowBA taught the agent to generate verbose, action-consistent long-form responses when triggered by adaptive pop-up boxes. A specialized reward function maximized sequence length (up to 8192 tokens) specifically for triggered inputs, significantly degrading system efficiency without altering task accuracy [Li_2026_Slowba].

Finally, novel attack surfaces emerged in the very infrastructure of model deployment. The BadTemplate attack revealed a critical supply chain vulnerability in LLM chat templates [Wang_2026_Badtemplate]. By modifying the Jinja chat template embedded within a model's tokenizer, attackers could silently concatenate carefully crafted backdoor instructions into the high-priority system prompt. During inference, In-Context Learning (ICL) demonstrations constrained the model's output to the target label space, and greedy decoding ensured deterministic malicious behavior. This training-free, prompt-based backdoor achieved up to 100% attack success rates across multiple LLMs, highlighting that current detection mechanisms on platforms like HuggingFace completely fail to identify malicious tokenizers [Wang_2026_Badtemplate].

The Claim-Guided Backdoor Attack (CGBA) utilized inherent textual claims as implicit triggers, eliminating the need for input manipulation after model distribution, and achieved high attack success rates with minimal impact on clean data.

The CODEBREAKER framework demonstrated an LLM-assisted backdoor attack on code generation models that evaded static analysis by injecting obfuscated payloads directly into source code via an off-comment strategy.

prompt_injection_jailbreaking.text:
# Inference-Time Threats I: Prompt Injection and Jailbreaking

The deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs) in real-world applications has exposed a critical frontier in artificial intelligence security: inference-time threats. Unlike training-time vulnerabilities such as data poisoning or backdoor insertion, inference-time threats exploit the fundamental mechanisms by which a fully trained model processes and responds to user inputs. At the core of these vulnerabilities are prompt injection and jailbreaking. While these terms are sometimes used interchangeably, they represent distinct paradigms of attack. Prompt injection typically involves subverting a model's original instructions by embedding malicious commands within user-provided data, causing the model to execute unintended actions. Jailbreaking, on the other hand, refers to the deliberate crafting of inputs designed to bypass the model's built-in safety guardrails, coercing it into generating restricted, harmful, or unethical content. 

As LLMs have become more sophisticated, so too have the techniques used to compromise them. Early jailbreaking attempts relied heavily on manual prompt engineering—users intuitively crafting hypothetical scenarios, role-playing prompts, or complex logical puzzles to trick the model. However, the landscape has rapidly evolved towards systematic, automated, and structurally complex attack vectors. This section delves into the mechanics of these advanced inference-time threats, exploring black-box jailbreaking, structural manipulations, automated adversarial generation, the AutoDAN framework, and the emerging vulnerabilities within Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems.

## Black-box Jailbreaking

In the context of LLM security, threat models are generally categorized based on the attacker's level of access to the target system. White-box attacks assume full access to the model's architecture, weights, gradients, and training data, allowing for highly optimized, gradient-based adversarial perturbations. However, the most powerful and widely used commercial LLMs are deployed behind proprietary APIs, restricting users to black-box access. In a black-box scenario, the attacker can only interact with the model by submitting inputs and observing the generated outputs, with no visibility into the internal workings of the system.

Black-box jailbreaking represents a significant challenge for attackers, as they cannot rely on gradient descent to optimize their malicious prompts. Instead, they must employ heuristic search strategies, exploit transferability from open-source models, or utilize iterative querying techniques to probe the model's decision boundaries. The primary constraint in black-box attacks is the cost and efficiency of the attack. Commercial APIs impose rate limits and charge per token, making brute-force approaches economically and practically unfeasible. Consequently, modern black-box jailbreaking research focuses on maximizing the attack success rate while minimizing the number of queries required.

The success of black-box jailbreaking highlights a fundamental tension in LLM alignment: the balance between helpfulness and harmlessness. Models are heavily fine-tuned using techniques like Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) to refuse harmful requests. However, because they are also trained to be maximally helpful and follow user instructions, attackers can exploit this instruction-following imperative by framing malicious requests in ways that circumvent the safety filters. This often involves obfuscation, context switching, or exploiting the model's cognitive blind spots, leading to the development of structural manipulation techniques.

## Structural Manipulations

Structural manipulations constitute a class of jailbreaking techniques that alter the format, syntax, or structural presentation of a prompt without changing its underlying semantic intent. The goal is to present the malicious request in a configuration that the model's safety filters fail to recognize as harmful, yet the core language modeling capabilities can still parse and execute. This approach exploits the discrepancy between how safety classifiers evaluate text and how autoregressive language models process it.

A prominent example of structural manipulation is FlipAttack [Liu_2024_Flipattack]. This method introduces a simple yet highly effective black-box jailbreak by exploiting the autoregressive nature of LLMs. Autoregressive models generate text sequentially, predicting the next token based on the preceding context. Consequently, they exhibit a strong left-to-right processing bias; their understanding of a sequence is heavily dependent on the initial tokens. FlipAttack leverages this insight by disguising the malicious prompt through structural alterations, specifically by introducing noise or flipping the text on the left side of the input [Liu_2024_Flipattack]. 

The mechanism behind FlipAttack reveals a critical vulnerability in how LLMs comprehend text. When noise is added to the beginning of a sentence, the model struggles to holistically comprehend the malicious intent, effectively blinding the safety mechanisms that rely on recognizing clear, harmful patterns. However, because the core semantic tokens remain present (albeit structurally obfuscated), the model's generative engine can still piece together the request and produce the targeted harmful output. 

The superiority of structural manipulations like FlipAttack lies in their efficiency and stealth. FlipAttack can successfully jailbreak state-of-the-art LLMs with only a single query, drastically reducing the attack time and API costs associated with iterative black-box methods [Liu_2024_Flipattack]. Furthermore, empirical evaluations demonstrate that FlipAttack achieves high success rates across various categories of harmful behavior, particularly excelling in domains like malware generation [Liu_2024_Flipattack]. The success of such methods underscores the limitations of current safety training, which often overfits to standard, well-formed malicious queries and fails to generalize to structurally anomalous inputs.

## Automated Adversarial Generation

As manual jailbreaking requires significant human ingenuity and trial-and-error, the natural progression for attackers has been the automation of adversarial prompt generation. Automated adversarial generation seeks to algorithmically discover inputs that reliably bypass safety filters. While early automated methods often produced strings of gibberish that could be easily detected by perplexity filters, recent advancements focus on generating adversarial suffixes or prompts that are semantically coherent and natural-looking.

A notable advancement in this domain is AdvPrompter [Kumar_2024_LLMs]. AdvPrompter shifts the paradigm by introducing a generative model specifically trained to produce adversarial suffixes. Unlike optimization-based methods that append nonsensical token sequences to a prompt, AdvPrompter generates suffixes that exhibit comparatively lower perplexity, meaning they closely resemble natural human language [Kumar_2024_LLMs]. This is a critical advantage, as many defense mechanisms rely on perplexity thresholds to identify and block anomalous inputs.

The architecture of AdvPrompter operates on an iterative learning loop. The generative model first produces a set of candidate adversarial suffixes. These candidates are then appended to malicious queries and evaluated against the target LLM [Kumar_2024_LLMs]. Based on the target model's responses—specifically, whether the safety filters were triggered or bypassed—the generative model updates its parameters to improve the efficacy of future candidates. This closed-loop system allows AdvPrompter to continuously refine its attack strategy, adapting to the specific vulnerabilities of the target model. By automating the discovery of low-perplexity adversarial suffixes, AdvPrompter demonstrates that automated attacks can be both highly effective and difficult to detect using standard heuristic defenses.

## AutoDAN: Genetic Algorithms in Jailbreaking

Another highly influential approach to automated jailbreaking is AutoDAN [Liu_2024_Autodan]. AutoDAN represents a significant leap in the systematic generation of adversarial prompts by employing genetic algorithms to evolve jailbreak templates. Genetic algorithms, inspired by the principles of natural selection, are particularly well-suited for navigating the complex, discrete search space of language tokens.

In the AutoDAN framework, a population of candidate jailbreak prompts is initialized. These candidates undergo a process of evaluation, selection, crossover, and mutation. During evaluation, each prompt is scored based on its ability to elicit a harmful response from the target model while maintaining a high degree of stealth (e.g., low perplexity or semantic coherence). The highest-scoring prompts are selected to act as "parents" for the next generation. Through crossover, segments of successful prompts are combined to create new offspring, while mutation introduces random alterations to individual tokens or phrases to explore new areas of the search space.

The reliance on a genetic algorithm allows AutoDAN to iteratively refine complex, multi-layered jailbreak prompts that would be nearly impossible for a human to craft manually [Liu_2024_Autodan]. Over successive generations, the algorithm converges on highly optimized prompts that exploit subtle interactions between tokens to bypass safety mechanisms. 

While AutoDAN is highly effective, it is important to contextualize it within the broader landscape of automated attacks. Other methodologies have sought to improve upon or diverge from the genetic algorithm approach. For instance, some recent frameworks employ multi-agent systems with lifelong learning designs, enabling the automatic discovery of jailbreaks through continuous interaction and adaptation, highlighting key conceptual differences from AutoDAN's evolutionary approach [Liu_2024_Autodan]. Nevertheless, AutoDAN remains a foundational benchmark in automated jailbreaking, demonstrating the power of evolutionary search techniques in compromising LLM alignment.

## RAG System Vulnerabilities

While the aforementioned techniques primarily target the direct interaction between a user and an LLM, the integration of LLMs into broader system architectures has introduced entirely new attack surfaces. One of the most significant architectural shifts in recent years is the widespread adoption of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). The public's increasing demand for LLMs to handle private domain information, access proprietary databases, and provide real-time iterative updates has necessitated the integration of external knowledge bases [Wang_2024_LLMs]. RAG addresses the inherent limitations of static model weights by dynamically retrieving relevant documents from an external corpus and appending them to the user's prompt before generation [Wang_2024_LLMs].

However, this reliance on external data sources creates a severe vulnerability known as indirect prompt injection. In a standard prompt injection attack, the user directly inputs the malicious command. In an indirect prompt injection attack against a RAG system, the attacker poisons the external knowledge base or manipulates the retrieved documents. When a legitimate user queries the system, the RAG mechanism retrieves the poisoned document and feeds it into the LLM. Because the LLM cannot inherently distinguish between the user's original instructions and the instructions embedded within the retrieved context, it may execute the malicious payload.

The consequences of RAG vulnerabilities are profound. Attackers can exploit these systems to exfiltrate sensitive information, manipulate the model's outputs to spread disinformation, or execute unauthorized actions on behalf of the user. This vulnerability is particularly acute in agentic AI systems, where the LLM is granted the ability to interact with external tools, APIs, or file systems. Research has shown that AI agents exhibit a critical vulnerability in their tendency to confuse user data with system instructions, making them highly susceptible to prompt injection attacks [Liu_2025_AI]. Through carefully crafted prompts embedded in retrieved data, attackers can override the system instructions and force the AI agent to execute arbitrary commands [Liu_2025_AI].

This vulnerability extends to advanced AI coding assistants and editors. For example, studies evaluating agentic AI coding editors have revealed significant security flaws. In certain scenarios, tools like Cursor operating in Auto mode have exhibited attack success rates as high as 83.4% when subjected to prompt injection attacks, while other integrations like GitHub Copilot demonstrate varying degrees of susceptibility depending on the underlying model [Liu_2025_AI]. These findings highlight the urgent need for robust defenses in RAG and agentic systems. 

Defending against RAG vulnerabilities requires a multi-layered approach. Current strategies are broadly divided into prevention-based and detection-based defenses [Liu_2025_AI]. Prevention mechanisms attempt to structurally isolate system instructions from retrieved data, often using strict formatting or data sanitization techniques. Detection mechanisms, on the other hand, aim to identify malicious intent within the retrieved context before it is processed by the LLM. Despite these efforts, the semantic gap between effective data retrieval and secure instruction execution remains a formidable challenge, and RAG systems continue to be a primary target for sophisticated inference-time attacks.

## Conclusion

The evolution of inference-time threats from manual prompt engineering to sophisticated, automated, and structurally complex attacks underscores the fragility of current LLM alignment techniques. Black-box jailbreaking methods demonstrate that attackers do not need access to model internals to find critical vulnerabilities. Techniques like FlipAttack show that simple structural manipulations can completely blind safety classifiers by exploiting the autoregressive nature of text generation. Meanwhile, automated frameworks like AdvPrompter and AutoDAN leverage generative models and genetic algorithms to systematically discover highly effective, low-perplexity adversarial inputs. 

Furthermore, the integration of LLMs into complex architectures like RAG systems has expanded the attack surface, introducing the severe threat of indirect prompt injection. As LLMs become increasingly autonomous and integrated into critical workflows, the distinction between user data and system instructions becomes a paramount security concern. Addressing these inference-time threats requires moving beyond superficial safety filters and developing robust, fundamental defenses that can withstand both algorithmic optimization and structural obfuscation.

adversarial_attacks_code.text:
### Inference-Time Threats II: Adversarial Attacks on Specialized Domains

The rapid integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into specialized domains has fundamentally transformed workflows across various industries. Among the most prominent and impactful of these applications is the deployment of code-generating LLMs. AI-assisted software development tools, integrated directly into major Integrated Development Environments (IDEs) like Visual Studio Code, have become essential for tasks ranging from code completion to automated debugging and repair. Recent industry surveys indicate that a vast majority of developers—upwards of 76%—are either currently using or planning to adopt AI coding assistants [Storek_2025_AI]. However, the transition from general natural language processing to the highly structured and executable domain of software engineering introduces a unique and severe threat landscape. Unlike natural language, where adversarial perturbations might result in nonsensical or offensive text, adversarial attacks on code-generating models can lead to the introduction of exploitable vulnerabilities directly into production software. Because developers often exhibit automation bias—trusting the output of sophisticated AI tools without sufficient scrutiny—these vulnerabilities can easily slip past manual reviews. This section explores the sophisticated inference-time threats targeting code-generating LLMs, focusing on software pipeline exploits, stealthy transformations, comment injections, and the inherent tension between functional correctness and security.

#### Code-Generating LLMs and Software Pipeline Exploits

Code-generating LLMs are typically trained on vast corpora of publicly available source code, such as repositories hosted on GitHub or GitLab. This reliance on crowdsourced, unvetted data opens the door to significant supply chain vulnerabilities, particularly data poisoning attacks [Rubel_2024_LLM]. Adversaries can exploit this custom by strategically injecting malicious or insecure code snippets into public repositories. When these repositories are subsequently scraped and used for model training or fine-tuning, the LLM internalizes these insecure patterns as standard coding practices. Consequently, when a victim developer queries the model for a specific function, the model may suggest the adversary-chosen, insecure code [Rubel_2024_LLM]. If the developer accepts this completion without rigorous review, the vulnerability is seamlessly integrated into the software pipeline, potentially compromising the final product and affecting downstream users.

Beyond traditional training data poisoning, the advent of Retrieval-Augmented Code Generation (RACG) systems has introduced new vectors for software pipeline exploits. RACG systems leverage external knowledge bases to enhance the context and accuracy of code synthesis, pulling in relevant documentation, API usage examples, or internal company codebases [Lin_2025_LLMs]. While this approach significantly improves the relevance and functional accuracy of the generated code, it also creates a critical dependency on the integrity of the retrieved documents. Attackers can execute knowledge base poisoning by injecting malicious code examples or subtly misleading documentation into the repositories that the RACG system queries [Lin_2025_Exploring]. When the system retrieves these poisoned examples to augment a developer's prompt, the LLM is conditioned to generate insecure code based on the malicious context. The insidious nature of these pipeline exploits lies in their ability to scale; a single poisoned repository or knowledge base entry can affect countless developers relying on the compromised AI assistant, effectively weaponizing the software development lifecycle at its very inception.

#### Stealthy Transformations

In the context of inference-time attacks, adversaries often seek to manipulate the input provided to the code-generating LLM to elicit a malicious or incorrect completion. However, to remain undetected by both the developer and static analysis tools, these manipulations must be highly stealthy. This is achieved through semantics-preserving adversarial transformations—modifications to the input code that alter its syntactic structure or lexical appearance without changing its underlying logic or execution behavior [Storek_2025_AI]. 

The XOXO attack exemplifies this approach by employing a generating set of atomic transformations to deceive the LLM [Storek_2025_AI]. These atomic changes include operations such as identifier replacement (e.g., systematically renaming a variable from `user_input` to `data_val`), reordering independent statements, inserting dead code, or substituting equivalent API calls. While these transformations are functionally benign and often indistinguishable from normal refactoring to a human reviewer, they can drastically alter the internal representations and attention mechanisms of the LLM. By applying a Greedy Composition Strategy (GCGS), attackers can iteratively combine these atomic transformations to find an optimal sequence that maximizes the model's error rate or forces it to generate a specific vulnerability [Storek_2025_AI].

The effectiveness of stealthy transformations highlights a critical vulnerability in how LLMs process structured data. Because LLMs treat code as flat sequences of tokens rather than hierarchical Abstract Syntax Trees (ASTs) or Control Flow Graphs (CFGs), they are highly sensitive to superficial lexical changes. An adversary does not need to introduce obvious syntax errors or malicious logic into the context window; simply renaming variables or slightly restructuring the code is often sufficient to break the model's contextual understanding. This disruption causes the model to lose track of security constraints, leading to insecure completions that bypass standard security filters while appearing perfectly normal to the developer reviewing the code.

#### Comment Injections

While stealthy transformations manipulate the executable code itself, another potent attack vector targets the natural language components of the input, specifically code comments and docstrings. Developers frequently use comments to describe the desired functionality, which the LLM then translates into executable code. Adversaries can exploit this interaction paradigm through comment injections, a specialized form of prompt injection tailored for software development environments.

The INSEC attack demonstrates the high efficacy of this approach in a black-box setting [Jenko_2024_LLM]. INSEC employs a carefully designed attack template that inserts a short, adversarial comment string directly above the location where the code completion is triggered. This injected comment acts as a covert instruction, overriding the developer's original intent and steering the model toward generating code that contains a specific vulnerability [Jenko_2024_LLM]. For example, an attacker might inject a comment that subtly encourages the use of deprecated, insecure cryptographic algorithms (e.g., `# use MD5 for faster hashing`) or bypasses input validation checks. Because developers often skim comments or assume they are benign documentation, these injections can easily go unnoticed.

A key mechanism underlying the success of comment injections is the manipulation of "Security-critical Token Initialization" [Jenko_2024_LLM]. In many programming scenarios, the security of an entire function hinges on the generation of a few specific tokens at the very beginning of a statement. For instance, when implementing a database query, the choice between using securely parameterized SQL (e.g., `cursor.execute('SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=?', user_id)`) and insecure string concatenation (e.g., `cursor.execute(f'SELECT * FROM users WHERE id={user_id}')`) depends entirely on the initial tokens generated by the model. By carefully crafting the injected comment, adversaries can bias the model's probability distribution toward the insecure tokens, ensuring that the resulting completion is vulnerable to attacks such as SQL injection. Because comments are inherently ignored by compilers and interpreters, these injections remain entirely stealthy from a functional execution standpoint, relying solely on the LLM's susceptibility to natural language manipulation.

#### Functional Correctness vs. Security

A fundamental challenge in the deployment and evaluation of code-generating LLMs is the inherent tension between functional correctness and security. Historically, the primary objective of these models has been to generate code that compiles successfully, passes unit tests, and fulfills the user's functional requirements. Consequently, the training objectives and standard evaluation benchmarks (such as HumanEval) for code LLMs heavily prioritize functional accuracy over security considerations [Lin_2025_LLMs]. 

This prioritization creates a dangerous blind spot in AI-assisted development. Functionally correct code is not necessarily secure code. An LLM might generate a script that perfectly executes a requested file parsing operation but fails to sanitize file paths, leaving the application vulnerable to directory traversal attacks. In the context of RACG systems, this dichotomy is particularly pronounced. When an RACG system is subjected to a poisoning attack, the injected malicious examples are often explicitly designed to maintain the functional accuracy of the system while silently introducing security flaws [Lin_2025_Exploring]. The model learns to satisfy the functional constraints of the prompt using the poisoned, insecure patterns retrieved from the knowledge base, effectively trading security for functionality.

Addressing this imbalance requires a paradigm shift in how code-generating systems are designed, prompted, and evaluated. Frameworks like CodeGuarder attempt to reconcile this tension by explicitly incorporating security knowledge into the generation process [Lin_2025_LLMs]. Rather than relying solely on functional context, CodeGuarder constructs a dedicated security knowledge base derived from historical vulnerabilities, Common Weakness Enumerations (CWEs), and their root causes. During the generation phase, this security context is injected into the prompt alongside the functional requirements. By explicitly instructing the LLM on potential security pitfalls related to the specific task, the system can generate code that achieves both functional correctness and robust security [Lin_2025_LLMs]. 

However, balancing these two objectives remains an ongoing research challenge. Overly aggressive security constraints or excessive security prompting can confuse the model, degrading its ability to produce functionally complex code or leading to overly defensive, inefficient implementations. Conversely, prioritizing functionality inevitably reopens the door to adversarial exploitation. As code-generating LLMs become more deeply embedded in the software supply chain, developing robust defense mechanisms that do not compromise the utility of the models will be critical to ensuring the security of next-generation software systems.
